findings.title: Cleanup job interval accidentally reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: Run's ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, and nothing in the PR description, changelog, or annotation-deadlock fix calls for that. This loop drives every cleanup job (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, and query-history row-limit enforcement), not just annotations. Each clean() call is allowed to run for up to 9 minutes, and the ticker is not drained, so once a job exceeds 1 minute the next run starts immediately and cleanup can become continuous. That is about a 10x increase in database load and works against the deadlock fix by running the annotation cleaner far more often. Restore the 10-minute interval unless a shorter schedule is an intentional, documented change.

findings.title: Cleanup debug traces left in at Error level and log every ID
findings.body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log at Error on every batch, including the terminating batch that finds nothing to delete: "Annotations to clean by time" (line 534), "cleaned annotations by time" (line 537), "Annotations to clean by count" (line 554), "cleaned annotations by count" (line 557), "Tags to clean" (line 576), and "cleaned tags" (line 579). These are not failures — the err field is logged after the error has already been returned, so it is always nil on the success path — but they are emitted as errors. Each line also dumps the full ID slice and the SQL condition. With a large AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize that is one enormous log record per batch, and with cleanup enabled it will fire on every cycle even when zero rows are deleted, triggering error-rate alerts and flooding log pipelines. Remove these traces, or drop them to Debug and do not log the ID list.

findings.title: SQLite ID inlining builds the IN list with quadratic string copies
findings.body: When the database is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, deleteByIDs inlines every ID into the DELETE statement by repeatedly doing values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v). Each iteration copies the whole string, so a batch of n IDs allocates O(n^2) bytes. That path exists specifically for large batches (the new test uses 32767). For n around 10k–30k this is hundreds of MB to multiple GB of temporary allocations and a multi-second pause on every batch, which can stall cleanup or OOM a small SQLite instance. Build the list with strings.Builder (or strings.Join of preformatted IDs) instead.
